claim: The vertebrate retina contains five classes of neurons: photoreceptors, horizontal cells, bipolar cells, amacrine cells, and retinal ganglion cells (RGCs).
source: The retina contains five classes of neurons – photoreceptors that sense light, three interneuronal classes (horizontal, bipolar, and amacrine cells) that process visual information, and retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) that pass the information to the rest of the brain through the optic nerve (Figure 1a; Masland, 2012).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Masland, 2012.

claim: The retina contains approximately 130 neuronal types in mouse and chick.
source: These classes can be divided into numerous types, ~130 in mouse and chick, each of which has characteristic morphological, physiological, and molecular properties, and plays distinct roles in information processing (Baden et al., 2016; Franke et al., 2017; Goetz et al., 2021; Macosko et al., 2015; Rheaume et al., 2018; Shekhar et al., 2016; Shekhar and Sanes, 2021; Tran et al., 2019; Yamagata et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Nearly all retinal neuronal types are distributed across the entire retina.
source: Remarkably, nearly all types are distributed across the entire retina (Kay et al., 2012; Keeley et al., 2020; Rockhill et al., 2000), so morphogen gradients, which play a critical role in other parts of the central nervous system (e.g., Sagner and Briscoe, 2019), cannot provide an explanation for retinal neuronal diversification (Marquardt and Gruss, 2002).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Kay et al., 2012; Keeley et al., 2020; Rockhill et al., 2000.

claim: Morphogen gradients cannot explain retinal neuronal diversification.
source: Remarkably, nearly all types are distributed across the entire retina (Kay et al., 2012; Keeley et al., 2020; Rockhill et al., 2000), so morphogen gradients, which play a critical role in other parts of the central nervous system (e.g., Sagner and Briscoe, 2019), cannot provide an explanation for retinal neuronal diversification (Marquardt and Gruss, 2002).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to Sagner and Briscoe, 2019 and Marquardt and Gruss, 2002.

claim: Single retinal progenitor cells (RPCs) can give rise to neurons of all classes as well as glia, and are therefore multipotential.
source: First, lineage tracing in rodents and frogs showed that single retinal progenitor cells (RPCs) can give rise to neurons of all classes as well as glia, and are therefore multipotential (Holt et al., 1988; Turner and Cepko, 1987; Turner et al., 1990; Wetts and Fraser, 1988).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to lineage tracing studies.

claim: The competence of multipotential RPCs to generate cells of particular classes changes over time, accounting for their sequential but overlapping birth windows.
source: Second, the competence of multipotential RPCs to generate cells of particular classes changes over time, accounting for their sequential (but overlapping) birth windows (Cepko, 2014; Livesey and Cepko, 2001).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to Cepko, 2014 and Livesey and Cepko, 2001.

claim: Competence of RPCs is probabilistic rather than deterministic, with stochastic factors accounting for variations in the distribution of cell classes generated by individual RPCs.
source: Third, competence is probabilistic rather than deterministic, with stochastic factors accounting for variations in the distribution of cell classes generated by individual RPCs (Boije et al., 2014; Gomes et al., 2011; Johnston and Desplan, 2010).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Boije et al., 2014; Gomes et al., 2011; Johnston and Desplan, 2010.

claim: Mouse RGCs can be divided into approximately 45 distinct types based on their patterns of gene expression.
source: However, they differ in molecular, morphological, and physiological details, which have led to their division into ~45 distinct types in mice (Baden et al., 2016; Bae et al., 2018; Goetz et al., 2021; Rheaume et al., 2018; Tran et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mouse RGCs are born between approximately embryonic days (E) 11 and 17.
source: Mouse RGCs are born between approximately embryonic days (E) 11 and 17 with newborn RGCs exiting the mitotic cycle near the apical margin, then migrating basally to form the ganglion cell layer (Dräger, 1985; Marcucci et al., 2019; Voinescu et al., 2009; Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text, supported by citations, and referenced to Figure 1b.

claim: More than 95% of RGCs in adult mouse retina are born after E12.8 and more than 85% before E16.
source: Reported birthdates differ among publications and are complicated by naturally occurring cell death and the central-peripheral developmental gradient, but a detailed analysis concludes that >95% of RGCs in adult mouse retina are born after E12.8 and >85% before E16 (Farah and Easter, 2005).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation to Farah and Easter, 2005.

claim: Some RGC axons reach retinorecipient areas by E15.
source: Shortly after they are born, RGCs extend axons through the optic nerve, with some reaching retinorecipient areas by E15 (Godement et al., 1984; Osterhout et al., 2011) and forming diverse projection patterns (Martersteck et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Godement et al., 1984 and Osterhout et al., 2011.

claim: During early postnatal life, RGCs extend dendrites apically into the inner plexiform layer of the retina, receiving synapses from amacrine cells by postnatal day (P)4 and bipolar cells a few days later.
source: During early postnatal life, they extend dendrites apically into the inner plexiform layer of the retina, receiving synapses from amacrine cells by postnatal day (P)4 and bipolar cells a few days later (Kim et al., 2010; Lefebvre et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to Kim et al., 2010 and Lefebvre et al., 2015.

claim: Light responses are detected in RGCs by P10 but image-forming vision does not begin until eye-opening, around P14.
source: Light responses are detected in RGCs by P10 but image-forming vision does not begin until eye-opening, around P14 (Hooks and Chen, 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to Hooks and Chen, 2020.

claim: A total of 98,452 single-cell transcriptomes with acceptable quality metrics were obtained.
source: We obtained a total of 98,452 single-cell transcriptomes with acceptable quality metrics (Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: 75,115 (76%) of the obtained single-cell transcriptomes were identified as RGCs based on their expression of canonical RGC markers.
source: Of these, we identified 75,115 (76%) as RGCs based on their expression of canonical RGC markers, including Rbpms (an RNA-binding protein) and Slc17a6 (the vesicular glutamate transporter VGLUT2) (Figure 1c–e, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by references to figures showing marker expression.

claim: Non-RGCs included amacrine cells (Tfap2a+ Tfap2b+), cone photoreceptors (Otx2+ Crx+), microglia (P2ry12+ C1qa+), anterior segment cells (Mgp+ Bgn+), and RPCs.
source: Non-RGCs included amacrine cells (Tfap2a+ Tfap2b+), cone photoreceptors (Otx2+ Crx+ ), microglia (P2ry12+ C1qa+), anterior segment cells (Mgp+ Bgn+ ), and RPCs.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with specific marker genes for each cell type.

claim: Approximately 5900–18,500 RGCs were recovered at each of the five time points.
source: Overall, we recovered ~5900–18,500 RGCs at each of the five time points.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Thy1 was effective at enriching RGCs at later stages.
source: Of the two surface markers used for enriching RGCs, Thy1 was effective at later stages as shown previously (Kay et al., 2011; Rheaume et al., 2018; Tran et al., 2019), whereas L1cam expression was more selective at E13 and E14 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations and figure references.

claim: L1cam expression was more selective at E13 and E14.
source: Of the two surface markers used for enriching RGCs, Thy1 was effective at later stages as shown previously (Kay et al., 2011; Rheaume et al., 2018; Tran et al., 2019), whereas L1cam expression was more selective at E13 and E14 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references.

claim: Identical clusters were observed with both Thy1 and L1cam enrichment methods at E13, E14, and E16, albeit with different frequencies.
source: However, identical clusters were observed with both methods at E13, E14, and E16, albeit with different frequencies.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The enrichment protocols increased the fractional yield of RGCs by more than 3× at E14 and E16 and by more than 100× at P0.
source: However, our enrichment protocols increased the fractional yield of RGCs by >3× at E14 and E16 and by >100× at P0 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h), which enabled us to resolve heterogeneity within this class at immature stages.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a figure reference.

claim: There were 10 transcriptionally defined precursor clusters at E13.
source: There were 10 transcriptionally defined precursor clusters at E13 (Figure 2b) before or at the peak time of RGC birth.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 2b.

claim: The number of discrete clusters increased from 10 at E13 to 12 at E14.
source: The number of discrete clusters increased only slightly by E14 (from 10 to 12; Figure 2c), arguing against a model in which the number of precursor types extrapolated back to 1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 2c.

claim: The number of transcriptionally defined clusters increased gradually between E13 and adulthood, reaching 45 only after P5.
source: Second, the number of transcriptionally defined clusters increased gradually, between E13 and adulthood, reaching 45 only after P5 (Figure 2b–g).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 2b-g.

claim: The transcriptomic variation among RGCs became increasingly discrete with age.
source: Third, the transcriptomic variation became increasingly discrete with age.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: The boundaries between RGC clusters become sharper as development proceeds.
source: From these trends, we conclude that the boundaries between RGC clusters become sharper as development proceeds (Figure 2i and j).
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion and supported by Figure 2i and j.

claim: Transcriptomic clusters of RGCs increase in number and distinctiveness over time, making it unlikely that RGC-type identity is fully specified at the progenitor stage.
source: Taken together, our results show that transcriptomic clusters of RGCs increase in number and distinctiveness over time, making it unlikely that RGC-type identity is fully specified at the progenitor stage.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the presented data.

claim: Correspondence between clusters at consecutive developmental stages fell between the two extreme models of specified and nonspecified diversification.
source: Correspondence fell between the two extremes (Figure 3d–h, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references.

claim: Both NCE and ARI metrics exhibited an increased degree of specificity with age.
source: Both metrics exhibited an increased degree of specificity with age (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 3b and c.

claim: The analysis of transcriptomic correspondence suggests that poorly specified relationships among transcriptomic clusters at early stages are gradually refined to yield increasingly specific associations at later stages.
source: Overall, this analysis of transcriptomic correspondence suggests that poorly specified relationships among transcriptomic clusters at early stages are gradually refined to yield increasingly specific associations at later stages.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the classification analysis.

claim: The majority of individual RGCs were multipotential at E13 and E14.
source: WOT indicated that the majority of individual RGCs were multipotential at E13 and E14.
evidence: The claim is directly stated based on WOT analysis.

claim: Immature RGCs were not totipotential: the average predicted potential (P) was 11.6 at E13, or approximately 25% of the maximum possible value of 45, and no RGCs had P > 30.
source: Of equal importance, immature RGCs were not totipotential: the average predicted potential (P) was 11.6 at E13, or ~25% of the maximum possible value of 45, and no RGCs had P > 30.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with specific numerical values.

claim: Single multipotential immature RGCs are biased in favor of particular groups of adult RGC types.
source: We conclude that single multipotential immature RGCs are biased in favor of particular groups of adult RGC types.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the potential analysis.

claim: Different pairs of RGC types decoupled at different rates.
source: Different pairs of types decoupled at different rates (Figure 5f).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 5f.

claim: Seven out of 45 RGC types are specified postnatally.
source: Based on this analysis, 7/45 types are specified postnatally.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated based on the specification time analysis.

claim: The inferred specification time was not correlated with adult frequency.
source: The inferred specification time was not correlated with adult frequency (Figure 5i).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 5i.

claim: RGC types emerge by asynchronous fate decoupling of multipotential precursors.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that RGC types emerge by asynchronous fate decoupling of multipotential precursors.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the fate coupling analysis.

claim: Eight transcription factors (TFs) are expressed by distinct groups of mature RGC types: Foxp2, Tbr1, Eomes, Neurod2, Irx3, Mafb, Tfap2d, and Bnc2.
source: As a step towards identifying candidate fate determinants, we identified eight TFs that are expressed by distinct groups of mature RGC types (Figure 6a, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a). Three of these are well-characterized RGC-selective TFs: Foxp2, expressed by five F-RGC types (Rousso et al., 2016); Tbr1, expressed by five T-RGC types (Liu et al., 2018); and Eomes (also known as Tbr2), expressed by seven types (Mao et al., 2020; Tran et al., 2019). The seven Eomes/Tbr2 types include the melanopsin-expressing intrinsically photosensitive (ip) RGC types (Berson et al., 2002). The remaining five were Neurod2, Irx3, Mafb, Tfap2d, and Bnc2, which label 8, 5, 4, 6, and 3 types, respectively.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations and figure references.

claim: Foxp2 is expressed by five F-RGC types.
source: Three of these are well-characterized RGC-selective TFs: Foxp2, expressed by five F-RGC types (Rousso et al., 2016); Tbr1, expressed by five T-RGC types (Liu et al., 2018); and Eomes (also known as Tbr2), expressed by seven types (Mao et al., 2020; Tran et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to Rousso et al., 2016.

claim: Tbr1 is expressed by five T-RGC types.
source: Three of these are well-characterized RGC-selective TFs: Foxp2, expressed by five F-RGC types (Rousso et al., 2016); Tbr1, expressed by five T-RGC types (Liu et al., 2018); and Eomes (also known as Tbr2), expressed by seven types (Mao et al., 2020; Tran et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2018.

claim: Eomes is expressed by seven RGC types.
source: Three of these are well-characterized RGC-selective TFs: Foxp2, expressed by five F-RGC types (Rousso et al., 2016); Tbr1, expressed by five T-RGC types (Liu et al., 2018); and Eomes (also known as Tbr2), expressed by seven types (Mao et al., 2020; Tran et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Mao et al., 2020 and Tran et al., 2019.

claim: The seven Eomes/Tbr2 types include the melanopsin-expressing intrinsically photosensitive (ip) RGC types.
source: The seven Eomes/Tbr2 types include the melanopsin-expressing intrinsically photosensitive (ip) RGC types (Berson et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to Berson et al., 2002.

claim: Together, 40/45 mature RGC types expressed at least one of the eight identified TFs in a manner that was, with a few exceptions, mutually exclusive.
source: Together, 40/45 mature types expressed at least one of these TFs in a manner that was, with a few exceptions, mutually exclusive.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The pairwise fate coupling among types from different subclasses was significantly lower than among types from the same subclass.
source: Consistent with their definition, the pairwise fate coupling among types from different subclasses was significantly lower than among types from the same subclass (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 6b.

claim: The average specification time for the Eomes group was E14.6.
source: The average specification time for the Eomes group was E14.6 (p<0.0001, Student's t-test, compared to the mean for all types), while that for the Mafb and Neurod2 groups were E16.9 (p<0.001) and E18.5 (p<0.0001), respectively.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with statistical significance.

claim: The average specification time for the Mafb group was E16.9.
source: The average specification time for the Eomes group was E14.6 (p<0.0001, Student's t-test, compared to the mean for all types), while that for the Mafb and Neurod2 groups were E16.9 (p<0.001) and E18.5 (p<0.0001), respectively.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with statistical significance.

claim: The average specification time for the Neurod2 group was E18.5.
source: The average specification time for the Eomes group was E14.6 (p<0.0001, Student's t-test, compared to the mean for all types), while that for the Mafb and Neurod2 groups were E16.9 (p<0.001) and E18.5 (p<0.0001), respectively.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with statistical significance.

claim: The early specification of the Eomes group is consistent with birthdating studies showing the average earlier birthdate of ipRGCs compared to all RGCs.
source: The early specification of the Eomes group is consistent with birthdating studies showing the average earlier birthdate of ipRGCs compared to all RGCs (McNeill et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to McNeill et al., 2011.

claim: The zinc-finger TF Zic2 is expressed in a subset of postmitotic RGCs in VT retina and is both necessary and sufficient for establishing their ipsilateral identity.
source: The zinc-finger TF Zic2 is expressed in a subset of postmitotic RGCs in VT retina and is both necessary and sufficient for establishing their ipsilateral identity (Herrera et al., 2003); transient dorsolateral I-RGCs do not express Zic2 (Pak et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Herrera et al., 2003 and Pak et al., 2004.

claim: Isl2 marks a subset of C-RGCs throughout the retina and appears to specify a contralateral identity in part by repressing Zic2.
source: Isl2 marks a subset of C-RGCs throughout the retina and appears to specify a contralateral identity in part by repressing Zic2 (Pak et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to Pak et al., 2004.

claim: Zic2 and Isl2 were expressed in a mutually exclusive fashion in RGC precursors between E13 and E16.
source: These two TFs were expressed in a mutually exclusive fashion in RGC precursors between E13 and E16 (Figure 7a); Zic2 was downregulated at later ages (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references.

claim: Zic2 expression at E13 correlated with Igfbp5 and Zic1, and anticorrelated with Igf1 and Fgf12.
source: Furthermore, Zic2 expression at E13 correlated with Igfbp5 and Zic1, and anticorrelated with Igf1 and Fgf12, consistent with recent reports (Wang et al., 2016; Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: The claim is directly stated, supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2016, and figure references.

claim: The expression of ipsilateral and contralateral gene signatures was anticorrelated at E13.
source: We scored each cell at E13 based on its expression of ipsilateral genes (Materials and methods), confirming that the expression of ipsilateral and contralateral gene signatures was anticorrelated (Figure 7c).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 7c.

claim: I-RGCs comprised 4.3% of adult RGCs.
source: We found that I-RGCs comprised 4.3% of adult RGCs, consistent with the range of 3–5% noted above.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with a specific percentage.

claim: At a fold change of ≥1.5, there were 59 differentially expressed (DE) genes at E13 and 89 at E14 between putative I-RGCs and C-RGCs.
source: At a fold change of ≥1.5, we found 59 differentially expressed (DE) genes at E13 and 89 at E14 (Figure 7e and f).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with specific numbers and supported by figure references.

claim: The number of genes differentially expressed between I- and C-RGCs decreased after E14, with 20, 9, and 0 significant genes at E16, P0, and P5, respectively.
source: The number of genes differentially expressed between I- and C-RGCs decreased after E14, with 20, 9, and 0 significant genes at E16, P0, and P5, respectively (Figure 7—figure supplement 1d and e), presumably reflecting the downregulation of axon guidance programs once retinorecipient targets have been reached (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with specific numbers and supported by figure references.

claim: At E13, putative I-RGCs were highly enriched in 2 of 10 clusters, comprising 38–40% of clusters 2 and 9, 9–14% of clusters 3 and 5, and <2% of the other six clusters.
source: At E13, putative I-RGCs were highly enriched in 2 of 10 clusters, comprising 38–40% of clusters 2 and 9, 9–14% of clusters 3 and 5, and <2% of the other six clusters (Figure 7d).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with specific percentages and supported by Figure 7d.

claim: In adults, RGCs expressing Tbr1, Mafb, Foxp2, and Neurod2 contained 3–4× more I-RGCs than RGCs expressing Eomes, Irx3, or Tfap2d.
source: In adults, RGCs expressing Tbr1, Mafb, Foxp2, and Neurod2 contained 3–4× more I-RGCs than RGCs expressing Eomes, Irx3, or Tfap2d.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with a specific fold-change.

claim: The results are consistent with previous observations that I-RGCs are morphologically and physiologically heterogenous but not uniformly distributed across types.
source: These results are consistent with previous observations that I-RGCs are morphologically and physiologically heterogenous but not uniformly distributed across types (Hong et al., 2011; Johnson et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Hong et al., 2011 and Johnson et al., 2021.

claim: The earliest precursor RGCs are multipotential and exhibit continuous variation in transcriptomic identity, then diversify into definitive types by a gradual process of fate restriction.
source: We conclude that the earliest precursor RGCs are multipotential and exhibit continuous variation in transcriptomic identity, then diversify into definitive types by a gradual process of fate restriction.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Similar strategies are used to generate cell classes from mitotically active progenitors and cell types from postmitotic precursors.
source: We suggest that, at least in this case, similar strategies are used to generate cell classes from mitotically active progenitors and cell types from postmitotic precursors.
evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the observed similarities.

claim: There is excellent concordance among RGC types defined by molecular, structural, and physiological criteria.
source: Fortunately, to the extent that they have been compared, there is excellent concordance among types defined by molecular, structural, and physiological criteria (Bae et al., 2018; Goetz et al., 2021; Tran et al., 2019; see http://www.rgc.types.org).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claim: RGCs of a single type exhibit a regular spacing, called a mosaic arrangement, in that they tend to avoid other members of the same cell type, whereas their association with members of other types is random.
source: Moreover, RGCs of a single type exhibit a regular spacing, called a mosaic arrangement, in that they tend to avoid other members of the same cell type, whereas their association with members of other types is random (Kay et al., 2012; Keeley et al., 2020; Rockhill et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Kay et al., 2012; Keeley et al., 2020; Rockhill et al., 2000.

claim: The adult RGC atlas is based on a detailed analysis of 35,699 cells.
source: First, the atlas is based on a detailed analysis of 35,699 cells and is therefore powered to detect types occurring at ~0.1% frequency (>40 cells per type; https://satijalab.org/howmanycells/).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with a specific cell count.

claim: The adult RGC atlas is powered to detect types occurring at approximately 0.1% frequency.
source: First, the atlas is based on a detailed analysis of 35,699 cells and is therefore powered to detect types occurring at ~0.1% frequency (>40 cells per type; https://satijalab.org/howmanycells/).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated based on power analysis.

claim: In a recent study profiling an additional approximately 120,000 RGCs, no additional types were identified.
source: Moreover, in the course of studies on responses of RGCs to injury, we recently profiled an additional ~120,000 cells (A. Jacobi, N. Tran, W Yan, and J.R.S, in preparation), without identifying additional types.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: RGCs have been classified by functional and structural properties, with 47 types defined by Bae et al., 2018, 42 by Goetz et al., 2021, and >32 by Baden et al., 2016.
source: Second, RGCs have now been classified by functional and structural properties, based on physiological responses to visual stimuli (Baden et al., 2016; Goetz et al., 2021) and serial section electron microscopy (Bae et al., 2018). The numbers of types defined in these ways (47 in Bae et al., 2018, 42 in Goetz et al., 2021, and >32 in Baden et al., 2016) match well to the 45–46 defined molecularly (Tran et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: Eomes is selectively expressed by ipRGCs and a few other types, and Eomes mutants fail to form ipRGCs although their retinas are normal in many respects.
source: Support for this idea is that there is already strong evidence that one such factor is a fate determinant in mouse: Eomes is selectively expressed by ipRGCs (and a few other types), and Eomes mutants fail to form ipRGCs although their retinas are normal in many respects (Mao et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to Mao et al., 2014.

claim: Assuming that WOT results are valid, there were few if any genes differentially expressed between the putative mature I- and C-RGCs, suggesting a model in which newborn RGCs are doubly specified by laterality and type, but once axonal choice has been made the laterality program is shut down.
source: Assuming that WOT results are valid – an assertion that can be tested directly in the future – this result suggests a model in which newborn RGCs are doubly specified – by laterality and type – but that once axonal choice has been made the laterality program is shut down.
evidence: The claim is stated as a suggested model based on the data.

claim: A recent study on primary sensory neurons reached the conclusion that newborn neurons in dorsal root ganglia are transcriptionally unspecialized and become type-restricted as development proceeds.
source: A recent study addressed this issue for primary sensory neurons and reached the conclusion that newborn neurons in dorsal root ganglia are transcriptionally unspecialized and become type-restricted as development proceeds (Sharma et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to Sharma et al., 2020.

claim: Both excitatory neuronal subclasses appear to diversify postmitotically in the mouse cerebral cortex.
source: Similarly, both excitatory neuronal subclasses appear to diversify postmitotically in the mouse cerebral cortex (Di Bella et al., 2021; Lodato and Arlotta, 2015), and there is suggestive evidence that the same is true for interneuronal subclasses (Wamsley and Fishell, 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Di Bella et al., 2021 and Lodato and Arlotta, 2015.

claim: There is suggestive evidence that interneuronal subclasses diversify postmitotically in the mouse cerebral cortex.
source: Similarly, both excitatory neuronal subclasses appear to diversify postmitotically in the mouse cerebral cortex (Di Bella et al., 2021; Lodato and Arlotta, 2015), and there is suggestive evidence that the same is true for interneuronal subclasses (Wamsley and Fishell, 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to Wamsley and Fishell, 2017.

claim: It is attractive to speculate that diversification may occur by a process of fate decoupling in subpopulations of distinct multipotential precursors in various neuronal systems.
source: In all of these cases, it is attractive to speculate that diversification may occur by a process of fate decoupling in subpopulations of distinct multipotential precursors, akin to that documented here for RGCs.
evidence: The claim is stated as speculation based on the study's findings.

claim: The study provides a computational framework for investigating diversification of neuronal types.
source: Our study provides a computational framework for investigating this issue.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.
